title: Colorado Sales Tax Guide: Rates, Home Rule, & Compliance
summary: Colorado has a 2.9% state sales tax rate plus local taxes that can bring the total to above 11%. See rates by city, nexus rules, and filing requirements.
body_markdown:
## Colorado sales tax at a glance


State taxing authority[Colorado Department of Revenue (DOR)](https://tax.colorado.gov/)


Colorado base sales tax rate 2.9%


Local tax rates Vary by city, county, and special district


Combined sales tax rate range Roughly 2.9% to 11.2%+ depending on location


Economic nexus threshold Over $100,000 in retail sales delivered into Colorado in the current or previous calendar year


Home rule state Yes, many cities administer their own sales tax separately


Streamlined Sales Tax member No


Website[tax.colorado.gov](https://tax.colorado.gov/)


Tax line (303) 238-7378


Most states have a centralized department of revenue that collects sales tax for the entire state and distributes it to local areas according to a predefined process. Home rule states, including Colorado, work differently.


Colorado is one of a few[home rule states](https://www.numeral.com/blog/home-rule-states-sales-tax) where local jurisdictions create and enforce their own sales tax rules. Home rule states give local areas significant power beyond sales tax, as each jurisdiction can write its own laws without state legislative approval.


As a home rule state, Colorado has dozens of local jurisdictions that set their own tax rates and requirements.


**So while Colorado has a low 2.9% statewide sales tax rate, local tax rates among the different home rule jurisdictions could bring the combined rate above 11% in some areas.**


The obligation to comply with local city tax requirements can also mean that sellers must separately register, file, and remit sales tax in dozens of locations.

## Colorado's home rule sales tax system


Colorado voters[authorized home rule governance](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/publications/home-rule-governance-colorado-20-16) for cities and towns starting in 1902 with the city and county of Denver. In 1970, a separate constitutional amendment also authorized home rule governance for all municipalities regardless of population size.


Home rule gives local governments the power to make key decisions that affect local matters. In most cases, local ordinances control even if state law differs, unless the issue relates to a matter of statewide concern.


Local cities and towns can do many things with their grant of power, including writing and administering their own separate sales tax codes that differ from the rules set by the state’s department of revenue.


Unfortunately for those selling into areas with home rule sales tax systems, this autonomy can be a major compliance issue for merchants. That's because each city, town, or district can separately:


- Establish the rules for when a seller has nexus with the area
- Require registration for sales tax collection once a seller has nexus
- Require a business with nexus to file local returns that are separate from state returns
- Set its own filing schedule, which may or may not coincide with the statewide schedule
- Require a seller to collect local tax at the district, town, or city's mandated rates and in accordance with its rules for what's taxable versus exempt


Not *every* local area chooses to do all these things. Some areas set their own city tax but allow the state to collect it.


However,[home rule cities](https://datastudio.google.com/reporting/b987b537-d28e-4429-a74d-c5db9ade7e9c/page/p_u5sbexersd) like Aurora, Boulder, Colorado Springs, Denver, Fort Collins, Greeley, and Lakewood have their own compliance obligations that businesses need to meet. So, sellers must understand their local rates, as well as their registration and filing requirements.


Home rule touches three parts of compliance covered below — the rate you charge, where you register, and where you file. Each of those sections refers back to this one.


## Colorado sales tax rates


In Colorado, there is a statewide sales tax rate of 2.9% that applies everywhere, including in home rule cities. However, the local taxes passed by counties, cities, and special districts stack on top of this 2.9% rate, with the amount depending on location.


The table below shows some examples of how this works. These rates are effective as of early August 2026. However, rates can change over time, and they vary by exact address, zip code, and home rule jurisdiction.


The table below is a reference that can help you to understand sales tax rates across Colorado. Colorado also has a[table of rates](https://datastudio.google.com/reporting/b987b537-d28e-4429-a74d-c5db9ade7e9c/page/p_u5sbexersd) for each local area statewide that you can use to look up the rate for each location, as well.


As the table illustrates, if a city spans multiple counties, two different rates in the city may apply depending on which county the area is in.

*Special districts are created in order to fund specific regional public services. For example, in Westminster, CO, the total special district tax is 1.10%. This rate is a combination of two distinct voter-approved initiatives:


- **RTD (Regional Transportation District)** . This is a 1.00% tax used to fund public transit, including regional buses, light rail, and commuter rail systems across all eight counties of the Denver metro area.
- **SCFD (Scientific & Cultural Facilities District)** . This is a 0.10% tax that charges one penny for every $10 spent. The revenue generated is distributed to nearly 300 cultural arts, music, theater, and science organizations throughout Colorado, including the Denver Art Museum and Denver Zoo.


Several cities apply different rates to food and liquor, including Boulder, Denver, Fort Collins, and Greeley. Check the[DR 1002](https://datastudio.google.com/u/0/reporting/b987b537-d28e-4429-a74d-c5db9ade7e9c/page/p_u5sbexersd) for the applicable rates before charging tax on food and liquor.


### How to calculate Colorado sales tax


To calculate sales tax in Colorado, start with the 2.9% state tax, then add county, city, and special-district taxes for the area you’re interested in.


For example, if you are selling in Arvada:


1. **Start with the Colorado state sales tax** of 2.9%.
2. **Add in the county tax,** which depends on where in the city you are located. It could be:


1. 0.75% in Adams County or
2. 0.5% in Jefferson County,


3. **Add in the city tax,** which is 3.46%
4. **Add in the special district tax,** which is 1.1%


For the portion of Arvada located in Adams County, the total tax is 2.9% + 0.75% + 3.46% + 1.1% = 8.21%.


For the portion of Arvada located in Jefferson County, the total tax is 2.9% + 0.5% + 3.46% + 1.1% = 7.96%.


As you can see, you must be *very* specific about the location because the correct sales tax rate can differ even within the same city.


### Origin vs. destination sourcing in Colorado


In some cases, the seller and buyer are in different areas of Colorado, or the[seller is outside Colorado](https://www.numeral.com/blog/do-you-charge-sales-tax-on-items-shipped-out-of-state) but selling to a buyer in Colorado. In these situations, you must determine if the buyer’s or the seller's sales tax rules apply.


This is called sourcing.


States that use the seller's location are called origin-based states, and states that use the buyer's location are called destination-based states. Colorado is a destination-based state. Tax is calculated based on where the buyer receives the product, not where the seller is located.


This means if a seller in Denver, with a 9.15% rate, sells to a buyer who receives the item in Pueblo with a 7.6% rate, the 7.6% rate applies.


## Colorado's retail delivery fee


In addition to the standard sales tax charged by the state, as well as in local areas throughout Colorado, there is also a[retail delivery fee](https://tax.colorado.gov/retail-delivery-fee) charged on certain deliveries. The fee applies when all of the following are true:


- A delivery includes at least one item of tangible personal property that is subject to sales or use tax.
- The delivery is made by motor vehicle to a location within Colorado, including when the taxable goods are mailed, shipped, or otherwise delivered by any motor vehicle.
- The seller's total Colorado retail sales in the prior year were[more than $500,000](https://tax.colorado.gov/retail-delivery-fee-retailers) , or they exceed $500,000 during the current calendar year (even if they had no sales the prior year) and the applicable 90-day period has passed.


The retail delivery fee is charged regardless of whether the buyer paid for shipping or not. The retailer or the[marketplace facilitator](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) responsible for collecting the[sales or use tax](https://www.numeral.com/blog/use-tax-vs-sales-tax) is responsible for remitting the retail delivery fee.


The amount due is a flat fee of[$0.31 per delivery](https://tax.colorado.gov/retail-delivery-fee-rates) as of July 1, 2026, regardless of the items being delivered. Colorado adjusts the fee for inflation each July.


This is separate from, and in addition to, state sales tax and any home rule city tax. In some self-collecting home rule jurisdictions, the fee itself is subject to sales tax.


Sellers who are responsible for collecting and remitting the fee must register for a separate[retail delivery account](https://tax.colorado.gov/retail-delivery-fee-accounts) .


## Sales tax nexus in Colorado


Merchants must collect and remit sales tax to state and local revenue departments in Colorado, but only if they have sufficient connections to the area. This is called establishing nexus.


There are[different types of nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-nexus) , and establishing *any* type of nexus makes a seller responsible for sales tax compliance. Here are the different kinds of[nexus a seller may establish in Colorado](https://www.numeral.com/nexus/colorado) :


Type of Nexus Threshold


**Physical**[Physical nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/physical-nexus) is established by any physical presence in Colorado, including an office, local employees, or inventory storage/a local warehouse (including inventory stored by a third party, such as Amazon for sellers who participate in Fulfillment by Amazon).


**Economic**[Economic nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/economic-nexus) is established once a seller has[over $100,000 in retail sales](https://tax.colorado.gov/out-of-state-businesses) delivered into Colorado in the current or previous calendar year.


Prior to[April 14, 2019](https://www.salestaxinstitute.com/resources/colorado-to-require-remote-seller-sales-tax-collection) , Colorado also defined economic nexus to include 200 or more transactions.


**Marketplace**[Marketplace facilitators](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) are online marketplaces that play an instrumental role in the sale of goods by a third party. Etsy and Amazon are examples.


An online platform that meets Colorado's statutory definition of a[marketplace facilitator](https://tax.colorado.gov/marketplace-facilitators) and that exceeds Colorado's $100,000 economic nexus threshold generally must collect and remit on behalf of its sellers.


**Affiliate** There's a presumption that[affiliate nexus](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/images/olls/crs2024-title-39.pdf) exists in Colorado when an out-of-state retailer has a relationship with an in-state affiliate that helps them build or maintain a market, shares a substantially similar business name, or helps to arrange deliveries and returns.


An exemption exists for small sellers outside of Colorado with less than $50,000 in cumulative gross receipts.


## What's taxable and exempt in Colorado


When you collect sales tax in Colorado, you only collect tax on non-exempt sales.


Most tangible personal property is subject to sales tax, but there are specific statewide exemptions.[Exempt products in Colorado](https://tax.dev.colorado.gov/sales-tax-exemptions-deductions) include:


- Food for home consumption, including food sold through vending machines
- Residential energy usage, including all gas, electricity, coal, wood, and fuel oil
- Eligible medical equipment and medicine
- Coins and precious metal bullion
- Some farm equipment
- Seeds, plants, and trees
- Pesticides
- Eligible machinery and machine tools
- Qualifying sales of low-emitting vehicles
- Eligible school-related sales
- Renewable energy components
- Space flight
- Aircraft and aircraft parts


Colorado[doesn't broadly tax most services](https://tax.colorado.gov/sales-tax-guide) , unlike some states. The exceptions are gas and electric service for commercial use and telephone and telegraph services.[SaaS is also not broadly subject to Colorado sales tax](https://www.numeral.com/blog/saas-sales-tax-colorado) .


However, because of home rule, a local jurisdiction may have different exemptions than the state. For example, while SaaS isn't subject to state tax throughout Colorado,[Denver does charge tax on software as a service](https://www.denvergov.org/files/assets/public/v/3/finance/documents/treasury/tax-guides/taxguidetopic18_software.pdf) .


## Registering for a Colorado sales tax license


If you have nexus in Colorado, the first step you'll need to take is to[register](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVMVaM6hs8zDVb2-oLKwKSUIOc5qXrMZoSI-vZaI5qk_dFzRUvPiZRs0hU-aLwLJi0KWjFVJlQjB7g7jZ-2IKRMTWkLTsIW9-eWQA0XPq6Gu7ZFGBMi8L00P992XXsu7KE) for a Colorado sales tax license. Registration is required no matter what type of nexus you have and is a prerequisite to being allowed to collect sales tax.


To register for a CO sales tax license, do the following:


1. **Gather the required information** . This includes your legal business name and DBA, your Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Social Security number, your business entity type, your company contact details, a list of products and services sold, your estimated monthly sales volume, and the date of your first Colorado sale.
2. **Visit**[MyBizColorado](https://mybiz.colorado.gov/intro) **to register online** . This allows you to receive your account number the day you apply and your license certificate within a few weeks. If you don't want to register online, you can also mail in Form CR-0100, but this takes several weeks to process. Or you can visit a[Taxpayer Service Center](https://tax.colorado.gov/visit-a-service-center) , which allows you to get a same-day temporary license.
3. **Pay your**[registration fee](https://tax.colorado.gov/standard-retail-license) **.** You'll pay up to $66 to register for your first location. This includes a $50 refundable deposit and a prorated license fee between $4 and $16 depending on when you apply.


Remember, this registers you *only* to collect statewide sales tax. You may also need to register separately in home rule locations.


In Boulder, for example, you'll need to[apply for a local business license](https://bouldercolorado.gov/services/business-licenses) .


### Registration requirements for remote sellers


In Colorado, retailers who have economic instead of physical nexus must start collecting Colorado sales tax when their retail sales into the state during the current calendar year are above $100,000.


The[Colorado Department of Revenue](https://tax.colorado.gov/out-of-state-businesses) states that:


> "The retailer must apply for and obtain a sales tax license and begin collecting Colorado sales tax by the first day of the first month commencing at least 90 days after the retailer's aggregate Colorado sales in the current year exceed $100,000. If the retailer's Colorado sales in the previous year exceed $100,000, the retailer is subject to Colorado sales tax licensing and collection requirements for the entire calendar year."


For example, under this rule, if on August 15, 2026, your Colorado sales cross $100,000 for the year for the first time, you need to be licensed and start collecting Colorado sales tax on December 1, 2026.


## Collecting Colorado sales tax


Once you have registered for sales tax in Colorado, you have the obligation to begin collecting the correct amount of tax due. Specifically, this means you must:


- Determine if the product is taxable or exempt.
- Apply the correct combined state, county, city, and special district rate based on where the item will be delivered or used (under Colorado's destination-based sourcing rules).
- Determine if tax must be paid on shipping or if you owe Colorado's retail delivery fee.


If you are selling on a marketplace that is considered a[marketplace facilitator](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) , the marketplace will take care of collecting tax on these sales for you. However, confirm that the platform actually is a marketplace facilitator. Amazon, Etsy, and eBay are.[Shopify is not](https://www.numeral.com/blog/is-shopify-a-marketplace-facilitator) .


You also need to know the rules for when you charge tax on shipping or delivery.


As[Numeral's shipping tax guide](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-shipping) explains, each jurisdiction makes its own rules for when you pay tax on shipping. And because Colorado is a home rule state, there are actually different rules depending on location within the state. For example:


- At the[state level](https://tax.colorado.gov/sales-use-tax-FAQ) , delivery charges are usually exempt from state sales tax if they are separable from the sale and listed separately on the invoice.
- In some locations, including in[Denver](https://www.denvergov.org/files/assets/public/v/2/finance/documents/treasury/tax-guides/taxguidetopic34_transportationcharges.pdf) , transportation and delivery charges of tangible personal property may be taxed.


Colorado's[retail delivery fee](https://tax.colorado.gov/retail-delivery-fee) described above may also apply in appropriate circumstances.


## Filing and paying Colorado sales tax


The Department of Revenue requires you to[file Colorado sales tax returns](https://www.numeral.com/blog/how-to-file-colorado-sales-tax-online) on a set schedule depending on your sales volume. If you are registered but do not have any reportable sales tax during your reporting period, you'll typically be required to submit $0 returns.


[Here are the rules](https://tax.colorado.gov/sales-tax-filing-information) for how often you must file based on the amount of sales tax you collect each month:


- **$50 or less per month.** Annual returns are required and due January 20.
- **Over $50 to under $1,100 per month** . Quarterly returns are required on the following dates: **‍**


- **January to March:** due April 20 **‍**


- **April to June:** due July 20
- ‍ **July to September:** due October 20 **‍**
- **October to December:** due January 20 **‍**


- **$1,100 or more per month** . Monthly returns are required and are due on the 20th day of the month following the reporting period. **‍**
- **Wholesale businesses** with an annual sales tax liability of $600 or less can file annually.


Businesses that pay more than $75,000 per year in state sales tax must pay by[Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT)](https://tax.colorado.gov/electronic-funds-transfer) . The payment is due the 20th day of the month following the reporting period.


Remember, these are deadlines for the statewide tax. Local home rule jurisdictions may have their own filing process.


In the past, Colorado offered a[sales tax vendor service fee](https://tax.colorado.gov/service-fee) , or vendor's fee, which allowed retailers to keep a small portion of the collected tax to compensate them for filing and remitting the tax. However, this rule was eliminated at the state level effective January 1, 2026.


### Filing through Colorado SUTS


Because compliance with home rule obligations can be so complicated, the Colorado Department of Revenue has established the[Sales & Use Tax System (SUTS)](https://tax.colorado.gov/SUTS-info) . The system allows you to:


- Look up sales and use tax rates by address
- Calculate tax rates on items with different tax rates in the same jurisdiction
- Remit all taxes in participating jurisdictions on a single platform and using a uniform remittance form
- Review a taxability and exemption matrix


The[remittance portal](https://suts.blt.govos.com/login) is the key feature of the SUTS because it allows you to file your retail sales tax returns not just for state taxes, but also for ** taxes due in participating home rule jurisdictions, all in one place.


You can find a very long list of[covered jurisdictions](https://tax.colorado.gov/SUTS-Jurisdictions) online. The list is broken up by participating city, municipality, county, and special district, and it includes but isn't limited to Broomfield, Denver, and more.


You must check the list to confirm the area where you are selling is a participating jurisdiction before you assume that using the SUTS is sufficient to fulfill your compliance obligations. And remember, not all areas participate, so you may still need to register separately for some places.


### Colorado sales tax penalties


According to the[Department of Revenue](https://tax.colorado.gov/tax-topics-penalties-and-interest) ,


> "The sales tax penalty for failure to file, pay, or correctly account for the tax due is the greater of $15 or a percentage of the unpaid, unaccounted, or incorrectly accounted tax equal to 10% plus 0.5% for each month the tax remains unpaid, not to exceed a total of 18%."


These penalties are current as of 2026. You do not want to face penalties and interest charges for unpaid tax, so make sure you understand and fulfill your obligations.


## Colorado sales tax audits


In Colorado, the Department of Revenue routinely selects businesses, including out-of-state companies doing business in Colorado, to determine if they are fulfilling their sales tax obligations.


If you are subject to a[sales tax audit](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZAHrOzAV6z163ED2G5V41qKHdYHRANzxQv4sLag12s4Q-DBHNuieRG_VZBxNBZ9IQLetrGpvpl40MD94UfnHXUjd091Cmuu83501EG4kbD0e7ccaekaYgWhLrButePoWtkYXCBQ) , you will likely need to provide details about reported sales, exemptions, and remittances. You can also contest findings through an appeals process.


The department’s[audit and protest guidance](https://tax.colorado.gov/protest-rights) explains the process, including how to contest findings and file an appeal.

## Colorado sales tax FAQs


Still need to know more? Here are the answers to frequently asked questions about Colorado sales tax.


### What is the sales tax rate in Colorado?


There is a statewide sales tax rate of 2.9% in Colorado, but Colorado is a home rule state, and local county, city, and special district taxes can apply. These combined taxes can bring rates in some areas of Colorado, like Winter Park, above 11%.


### What is home rule sales tax in Colorado?


Home rule means local areas in Colorado can make their own laws and regulations on local matters without input from the legislature. This includes making their own sales and use tax rules.


Because of home rule sales tax, sellers must understand the county, city, and special district taxes that apply in any location where they sell. The rates and requirements can differ from those in the county next door, so getting this correct is critical. Sellers may also have to register and remit taxes in multiple jurisdictions.


### What is Colorado's retail delivery fee?


Colorado's retail delivery fee is a flat fee of $0.31 per delivery charged when a delivery includes at least one taxable tangible item of personal property if the delivery is made by a motor vehicle to a location in Colorado, including when deliveries are mailed or shipped. The fee applies when the seller's total Colorado retail sales in the prior year were more than $500,000.


### Does Colorado have economic nexus?


Yes. Once an out-of-state business exceeds $100,000 in sales into Colorado, it must register and collect, but not immediately. Colorado requires the retailer to obtain a license and start collecting by the first day of the first month beginning at least 90 days after current-year sales exceed $100,000.


### Are services taxable in Colorado?


Colorado does not broadly charge tax on services, including on Software as a Service (SaaS). There are some limited exceptions to this, including gas and electric service for commercial use and both telephone and telegraph services.


Digital goods are different. Colorado taxes downloaded and streamed content as tangible personal property, and some home rule jurisdictions impose tax on more services, including Denver, which taxes SaaS.


### Do I need to register separately in Colorado's home rule cities?


You must register separately in many home rule cities if you establish nexus in a local area that requires it. Many jurisdictions in Colorado require a separate local sales tax license and require you to file returns there, in addition to registering and remitting returns to the state.
